label: Ammunition, fireworks, flares and explosives
summary: Homes, farms, boats and old military ranges can hold cartridges, fireworks, flares, forgotten dynamite and detonators, and unexploded military ordnance. Fire, heat and disturbance set them off, and age doesn't make them safe. Store everyday items cool, dry and apart; leave the rest where it lies.
signs: Military items such as shells, grenades, mortar bombs, rockets and flares, often old, corroded, missing parts, partly buried or underwater; they can look like a piece of pipe, an old muffler or a pop can, and can get less stable with age
Dynamite and detonators stored and forgotten on farms and rural properties
Cartridges and shotgun shells, boxed or loose, and packages, trailers or rail cars marked as explosives, Division 1.1 to 1.6
Road flares (fusees) with a striker cap, marine distress flares and smoke signals, and fireworks
Ammunition or flares that are wet, damaged, scorched, or have been through a fire or flood

Burn times: fusees carried on US commercial vehicles must be able to burn 30 minutes, wildland fusees (NFES 0105) burn 10, marine hand flares at least 1 minute. Marine flares expire 4 years after the date of manufacture stamped on each
do: Military-looking items: don't touch them or any rusted metal lying on the ground or in the water. Note where it is and go back the way you came
Old dynamite or detonators: don't touch or move them; take photos from where you stand if you want a record, and keep people away

Keep cartridges in their factory boxes, locked away from children, dry and below 65 °C (150 °F), not in a closed vehicle in the sun, and at least 4.6 m (15 ft) from flammable liquids, flammable solids and oxidisers
Store flares upright in a cool, dry, watertight container, away from sun, heat, fuel and anything that burns, with fusee caps left on
Lighting a road flare: hold it away from your body as you strike it, wear eye protection, use it outdoors only, and mind the molten flecks it throws
Marine hand flares: hold them clear of the boat and downwind, and don't look into the flame; read the maker's instructions first
Starting a fire with a fusee (wildland crews light fires with them): burn it out completely and throw the spent end into the fire, not into water, which unburned fusees contaminate with perchlorate
dont: Don't throw cartridges, flares, fireworks or explosives into a fire, burn barrel or the rubbish: cartridges burst and can throw primer cups and case bits, usually not over 15 m (50 ft), and flares thrown out with rubbish have exploded and seriously injured people

Don't fight a fire that has reached explosives or fireworks, or move anything that has been heated. For a rail car or trailer load the ERG says fragments can fly 1600 m (1 mile) from Division 1.1 to 1.3 and 800 m (1/2 mile) from 1.4 (1.4S: 15 m)
Don't use a radio transmitter within 100 m (330 ft) of electric detonators
Don't light road flares indoors, inside a vehicle, near spilled fuel, or beside fuel tankers (loaded or empty) or commercial vehicles that run on compressed gas
Don't relight or pick up a firework that didn't go off fully
Don't bury ammunition or dump it in water: it can be found years later, still live
ppe: Safety glasses or goggles when lighting or handling a burning flare
Leather gloves protect against sparks and moderate heat; the flare maker's SDS asks only for safety glasses or goggles in normal use
Against old explosives and military ordnance, distance is the protection: don't touch them, and leave
firstAid: Flare burns: cool with water and cover; for a burn to the eye, cover the eye and get medical help at once
Flare powder on skin: wash with soap and water for 15 minutes; in an eye, flush with plenty of water for at least 15 minutes, lifting the lids
Flare smoke breathed in: get to fresh air and rest
Hit by fragments: control bleeding and treat as on the Sharp edges card; burns as on Hot surfaces
